特倫比塔長號具有穿透力強、明亮刺激的音色，帶有高山號族樂器典型的金屬質感與尖銳特: The trembita has a bright, exciting timbre that carries strongly, with the metallic edge and sharpness typical of the alpine horn family. Its range is high and its volume loud, so that it carries a long way in open mountain country, which is precisely its function as a signalling instrument for mountain herders. The wooden resonating body gives a distinctive resonance, so that the timbre has both the warmth of a woodwind and the bright penetration of a brass instrument. Compared with the refinement of the trumpet, the trembita is rougher and more primitive; compared with the depth of the trombone, it is sharper and more direct. Its timbre, between national character and an archaic quality, makes it an indispensable musical symbol of the highland folk music of Ukraine, Poland and elsewhere.

The source does not state the materials of the mouthpiece, fingerholes or other parts; since it has no side holes, it sounds from the air column inside the wooden body, and no reed, membrane or metal fitting is recorded.

The trembita is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs classification number 423.121-12, a member of the wooden alpine horn family. The body is made from a long straight piece of pine or spruce, split and hollowed out and then joined, and wrapped on the outside with birch bark or willow hoops. It has no side holes and sounds from the natural harmonics, and its timbre is brighter than the alphorn's. It is found mainly in the Carpathians of western Ukraine, eastern Poland, Slovakia and northern Romania, where Hutsuls and Gorals use it for signals, to announce a death, a funeral or a wedding, and also to let shepherds communicate and guide their flocks and dogs.
特倫比塔長號的歷史脈絡主要與喀爾巴阡山居民有關。名稱可能源自羅馬尼亞語特里姆比察: The history of the trembita is tied mainly to the people of the Carpathians. The name may come from the Romanian trâmbița, under Slavic influence; in Poland there are also the names trombitа, bazuna and ligawka. For a long time it was a signalling instrument of the Hutsuls and Gorals, used to announce funerals and weddings, and for shepherds to keep in touch in the mountains and guide their flocks and dogs. Today it has entered Galician ethnographic bands and folk instrument orchestras, and it appeared in 2004 at the Eurovision Song Contest in Ruslana's performance; the Ukrainian band ONUKA also uses it. The Polish folk musician Józef Chmiel once made the longest, 8.35 metres, which is now kept in the Czech Republic.
特倫比塔長號的聆聽場合主要來自喀爾巴阡山區生活與現代舞臺。胡楚爾與戈拉爾居民過去: The trembita is heard mainly in the life of the Carpathian mountains and on the modern stage. Hutsul and Goral communities once used it to carry news of weddings and funerals, and for shepherding and mountain signals; today it is common in Galician ethnographic ensembles, and as an occasional instrument in the orchestras of Galician folk instruments. In 2004, at the Eurovision Song Contest, the Ukrainian winner Ruslana used the instrument in her performance of the song Wild Dances; the Ukrainian band ONUKA has also used it. Its sound, with no side holes and purely natural harmonics, makes demonstrations sound bright, with the air of mountain forests.
